headline: AI makes novel exploits cheap, rendering traditional security stacks obsolete
summary: AI agents are now autonomously discovering and exploiting zero-day vulnerabilities, drastically reducing the cost and time for attackers to create novel threats.
details: In October 2024, Google's Big Sleep AI found a memory-safety bug in SQLite. Nine months later, a newer version found another live bug, CVE-2025-6965, which Google shut down before exploitation. This marks the first time AI foiled a real exploit pre-landing.

Historically, finding novel exploits was expensive, requiring skilled human effort. AI has now significantly cut this "tax," making advanced attacks more accessible. This shift is evident in changing traffic patterns observed by honeypot companies.

XBOW, an autonomous pentester, topped HackerOne's US leaderboard in June 2025, submitting over 1,060 vulnerabilities. At DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge, autonomous systems found 18 unknown bugs and patched 11 in 45 minutes, averaging $152 per patch.

A UIUC team demonstrated GPT-4 exploiting 87% of 15 real one-day CVEs using only public descriptions, while other models failed. These capabilities are no longer theoretical, with prices falling and real-world applications emerging.

Anthropic detected a Chinese state group in November 2025 using their own model to execute 80-90% of an espionage operation. Google's threat intel also documented malware that uses an LLM at runtime to rewrite itself, evading antivirus, deployed against Ukraine.

Traditional signature-based security, including firewalls, WAFs, and EDR, relies on matching known-bad patterns. This approach is inherently flawed against novel exploits, as a signature cannot exist for a pattern never seen before.

The average time from bug disclosure to exploitation dropped from 63 days in 2018 to 5 days in 2023. In 2023, 70% of exploited vulnerabilities were zero-days, meaning no signature existed prior to the attack.

AI is now manufacturing these "never-seen patterns" at a cost affordable to mid-tier criminals. This renders signature-matching defenses increasingly ineffective by design, creating a critical gap in security.

The solution lies in deception-based security, like honeypots, which detect trespass by observing behavior rather than signatures. By deploying services no legitimate user would touch, any connection signals hostile intent without false positives.

headline_marked: [[AI coding assistants introduce vulnerabilities]] in 45% of tasks, 2.74x more than human code
headline: AI coding assistants introduce vulnerabilities in 45% of tasks, 2.74x more than human code
summary: While AI coding boosts productivity, new reports reveal a significant rise in security vulnerabilities. AI-generated code contains 2.74x more flaws than human-written code, creating a rapidly compounding security debt for organizations.
details: AI coding assistants are driving significant productivity gains, with 89% of engineering leaders reporting improvements. However, this comes with a hidden and rapidly compounding cost: a surge in security debt due to developers integrating AI output with minimal oversight, a practice dubbed "vibe coding."

This dynamic creates a "comprehension gap," as developers integrate code they don't fully understand. Veracode's 2025 GenAI Code Security Report found that AI introduces a security vulnerability in 45% of coding tasks, picking an insecure option nearly half the time.

Further analysis showed AI-generated code carries 2.74x more vulnerabilities than human-written code, including 1.91x more insecure direct object references and 1.88x more improper password-handling flaws. Security pass rates remain stuck around 55%, with Java being the riskiest language at a 72% failure rate.

AI models prioritize functional correctness over security, leading to stark enterprise data. Apiiro's research found AI-assisted developers committed code 3-4 times faster, but monthly security findings rose tenfold, from 1,000 to over 10,000 in six months.

Crucially, the nature of vulnerabilities shifted: trivial errors dropped, but dangerous architectural flaws increased significantly. Privilege escalation paths rose 322%, and architectural design flaws rose 153%, with AI-assisted developers exposing cloud credentials at nearly twice the rate of their non-AI peers. Iterating on AI-generated code does not self-correct these underlying problems.
